n: Merodach-baladan, a Chaldean leader who repeatedly rebelled against Assyria, sends a get-well gift to Hezekiah. The gesture was likely political too—he wanted allies against Assyria.

f.g: Babylonian Marduk-apla-iddina II; he ruled Babylon twice (about 721–710 and 703 BC).

n: Flattered, Hezekiah gives the envoys a full tour of his treasury and armory—everything. It was a proud display, and perhaps a quiet bid to join an anti-Assyrian alliance.

f.g: Fine oil, a valuable trade item.

n: Isaiah arrives and questions the king. Hezekiah answers proudly that they came from far-off Babylon—as if that proved his importance.

f.g: Babylon lay about 500 miles (800 km) east of Jerusalem.

n: Isaiah asks what they saw. Hezekiah admits: everything. Earlier he had trusted God alone; here he seems to rely on impressing foreign powers.

f.w: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them

n: Isaiah prepares to deliver the Lord’s response.

A stunning prophecy: the day will come when everything in the palace will be carried to Babylon. At the time Babylon was a minor power under Assyria’s thumb; about a century later (586 BC) Babylon did exactly this.
Some of Hezekiah’s descendants will be taken as captives to serve in the Babylonian court. Daniel and his friends were among the young men of royal and noble Judah later taken there.

f.g: Court officials; the Hebrew word can mean high officers as well as castrated servants.

f.w: in the palace of the king of Babylon

n: Hezekiah accepts the word as good, relieved that peace will last in his lifetime. Some read this as humble submission; others see a hint of shortsightedness. This chapter bridges to Isaiah 40, which speaks comfort to those later exiled in Babylon.

f.w: Good is the word of the LORD
f.g: An acceptance of God’s judgment as just.

f.w: peace and truth in my days
